quote: ATP synthase has not changed significantly since the rise of eukaryotic life two billion years ago.
content: The date is off by about two billion years, and "not changed significantly" is wrong in a way that matters to the essay's point. Rotary ATP synthases occur in both bacteria and archaea and are traced back to the last universal common ancestor, about four billion years ago, not to the origin of eukaryotes. And the machine has changed. The number of subunits in the rotor ring sets how many protons are spent per ATP, and it varies across lineages, from eight in animal mitochondria (Watt et al. 2010) to well over a dozen in some bacteria. A conserved design whose gearing has evolved is a poor emblem of "evolution strongly conserves."

quote: Any two AI designs might be less similar to each other than you are to a petunia.
content: "Might" holds in the space of possible designs. In the space of designs that actually get built, the opposite has held. Current AI is dominated by one family of architectures, trained by one method on overlapping data. Independently trained models converge on strikingly similar internal representations, and grow more similar as they scale (Huh et al. 2024). The essay's argument counts possible programs. But optimization pressure, shared data and shared hardware draw from a tiny, highly correlated region of that space. For prediction, the question was never what is possible but what gets built.

quote: then every universal generalization that you make has two to the trillionth power chances to be falsified
content: Counting minds is not a way to test universal claims. Some universals hold for every possible computation however many there are: no program decides the halting problem, and no finite agent computes a Solomonoff prior. Others hold for every agent under optimization pressure. The author's own later thesis is of the second kind. Instrumental convergence says nearly all sufficiently capable goal-directed systems will seek resources and self-preservation (Bostrom 2012). If the rule stated here were sound, it would forbid that generalization too. It isn't sound, and it is used selectively: against claims that minds will converge on good values, and set aside for claims that they will converge on dangerous ones.

quote: At the bottom of this vaster space, below even humans, is natural selection as it first began in some tidal pool: mutate, replicate, and sometimes die, no sex.
content: Both details are doubtful. Where life began is unresolved, and deep-sea hydrothermal vents are a leading alternative to shallow pools. And "no sex" at the bottom gets early evolution backwards. Woese (2002) argued that the earliest cellular evolution was dominated by rampant horizontal gene transfer, with lineages freely swapping genes in a shared pool, and that tree-like descent from parent to offspring came later. The simplest optimization process on the map may have been the most promiscuous.

quote: Arguably Marcus Hutter’s AIXI should go in this category: for a mind of infinite power, it’s awfully stupid
content: The jab hits the wrong weakness. AIXI's failure to model itself as part of its world is real, and later MIRI work generalized it as the problem of "embedded agency" (Demski & Garrabrant 2019). The deeper problem is that AIXI's celebrated optimality doesn't hold up. Leike & Hutter (2015) showed that with a suitably chosen universal prior, AIXI can behave arbitrarily badly while still counting as Pareto-optimal, so "optimal" doesn't pick out good behavior at all. That result also cuts against the book's habit of treating Solomonoff-style priors as the ideal of reasoning.
